correctness.summary: stackalloc int[1000001] allocates ~3.8 MB on the stack, far exceeding the default 1 MB managed-thread stack, causing a StackOverflowException (uncatchable, process abort) on every single invocation regardless of input size.
correctness.triggeringInput: Any valid call, e.g. n=1, qCount=1, uCount=0 with a single query {L=0,R=0,T=0,Id=0} on the default thread (1 MB stack). Run never returns; the process is torn down by stack overflow before the loop executes.
correctness.rootCause: The frequency table is allocated with stackalloc int[1000001] = 1000001*4 = 4,000,004 bytes. The default .NET thread stack is 1 MB, so reserving ~3.8 MB for a single local guarantees a stack overflow at method entry. This is not a precondition the caller can satisfy (there is no parameter controlling the allocation size), so the method is unusable for all inputs, not just large value ranges.
correctness.suggestedFix: Do not stackalloc a fixed million-entry table. Either (a) take the frequency buffer as an int* freq parameter supplied by the caller (heap/pooled), sized to the actual value range, or (b) size the allocation to the real maximum value present in arr (passed as maxVal+1) and heap-allocate when it is large. The value-range assumption should also be a documented contract on a caller-provided buffer rather than a hardcoded 1000001.

perf.summary: Replace O(q^2) selection-style sort with an O(q log q) quicksort like the one already in MoSort.
perf.currentCost: Nested i/j loops: for every i scans all j>i, swapping. That is q*(q-1)/2 comparisons = Theta(q^2). For q=1e5 this is ~5e9 CompareQueries calls, each doing 3 integer divisions and CompareTo — catastrophic vs the rest of the algorithm which is roughly O((n+q) * n^{2/3}).
perf.proposedChange: Implement an in-place iterative/recursive median-of-middle quicksort over the Query3D* array (mirroring MoAlgorithm.MoSort.QuickSort) using CompareQueries (made branch-comparison) as the predicate. Precompute block(L)=L/blk into the comparison via a Less() returning bool to avoid CompareTo. Optionally keep insertion sort only for sub-ranges < ~16 elements.
perf.rationale: Asymptotic improvement from Theta(q^2) to Theta(q log q). This is the single dominant cost for large q; the sort currently can dwarf the entire Mo traversal.
perf.risk: Quicksort is not stable, but Mo's sort does not require stability (ties broken fully by the comparator on L-block, R-block, T). Must ensure the comparator gives a total order (it does: L-block, then R-block, then T). Recursion depth worst-case O(q); use median-of-three or the existing left+(right-left)>>1 pivot plus tail recursion on the larger side to bound stack.

perf.summary: stackalloc int[1000001] (~4 MB) on the stack risks stack overflow and is not Burst/mobile-friendly; take freq as a caller-provided pointer.
perf.currentCost: int* freq = stackalloc int[1000001] allocates ~4,000,004 bytes on the stack per Run call. Default thread stack is ~1 MB; this overflows on most platforms, and on mobile (smaller stacks) it is guaranteed UB. It is also not zero-cost — the runtime zero-inits 4 MB every call.
perf.proposedChange: Remove the stackalloc and add an int* freq parameter (and a maxVal/freqLen) to Run, matching the rest of the library's convention where the caller owns buffers (MoAlgorithm passes int* freq everywhere). Caller allocates once and reuses, pre-zeroed. Document that freq length must exceed max array/update value.
perf.rationale: Eliminates a multi-megabyte per-call stack allocation and its mandatory zeroing, removes stack-overflow risk on PC and mobile, and makes the function reusable without re-zeroing 4 MB each call. Aligns with the house buffer-ownership pattern.
perf.risk: API change (adds parameters) — breaks existing callers, but the current form is effectively broken anyway due to overflow. Caller must guarantee freq is large enough and zeroed; this matches the 'Unchecked Run assumes valid input' convention.

perf.summary: Per-comparison divisions and CompareTo calls are expensive in the hot sort comparator; precompute L/blk and R/blk once per query and compare branchlessly.
perf.currentCost: Each call does up to 4 integer divisions (a.L/blk, b.L/blk, a.R/blk, b.R/blk) plus int.CompareTo (a non-inlined-by-default method-call producing -1/0/1). In an O(q log q) sort this runs q log q times; divisions are ~20-40 cycles each on mobile ARM.
perf.proposedChange: Precompute each query's L-block once (store block index in Query3D.Id-adjacent scratch, or compute a parallel int* lblock array before sorting) so the comparator only compares precomputed ints. Replace a.X.CompareTo(b.X) with direct 'if (x!=y) return x<y' bool comparisons (return bool from a Less predicate). If blk is a power of two, L/blk becomes L>>log2(blk) (guard: L>=0, which holds for indices).
perf.rationale: Removes repeated divisions (compute L-block n times instead of ~n log n times) and replaces CompareTo call overhead with inlined integer compares, shortening the dependency chain in the innermost sort loop.
perf.risk: Shift replacement only valid when blk is a power of two and operands non-negative (array indices are >=0, so safe). Precomputing blocks needs a small parallel buffer or reuse of an existing field; must keep it in sync with any swaps (compute block-of-L, not block index, so it moves with the query).

perf.summary: Run mutates the caller's input arr in place via Apply/RevertUpdate, leaving arr in a non-deterministic final state; document or restore.
perf.currentCost: ApplyUpdate/RevertUpdate write arr[u.Pos] = NewVal/OldVal, so after Run the input array reflects whatever the last processed query's time was — a hidden side effect on caller data, not a pure query routine.
perf.proposedChange: Either document explicitly that arr is scratch/clobbered, or restore arr to its original state at the end by reverting curT back to 0 (the time-travel loop already supports this). For determinism, callers re-running Run on the same arr must reset it; making restoration explicit removes that footgun.
perf.rationale: Removes hidden mutable state leaking into caller buffers; makes Run idempotent/deterministic across repeated calls, which matters for a reusable library routine.
perf.risk: Restoring arr adds O(uCount) work at the end (cheap relative to the main loop). If callers intentionally rely on arr being updated, restoration changes observable behavior — so prefer documenting unless idempotency is desired. No correctness risk to ans[].
